hints: Focus on the phrase all types of transverse waves, which includes both electromagnetic waves and mechanical waves such as waves on a string or water surface.
Recall the defining geometry of a transverse wave: particle vibration is perpendicular to the direction of energy propagation, not parallel.
Compare speed and vacuum travel for different examples: light versus a string wave need different media and have very different speeds, but both can be reflected to superpose.
walkthrough: List what counts as transverse: electromagnetic waves such as light, plus mechanical waves such as waves on a stretched string and ripples on water.
State the definition: in a transverse wave the displacement vibration is perpendicular to the direction of propagation of energy, so the parallel-vibration statement describes longitudinal waves.

Test speed and medium: wave speed $v = f\lambda$ depends on the properties of the medium, so light, water and string waves do not share one speed, and only electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum.

Recall superposition: when any progressive wave is reflected, the incident and reflected waves of same frequency superpose to give a stationary wave, and this applies to all transverse waves given suitable reflection.
Therefore the only statement true for every transverse type is that stationary waves can be formed. This is option C.

options.A: Speed depends on the medium and wave type, for example light at $3.0 \times 10^8 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ in vacuum is much faster than a transverse wave on a string.
options.B: Parallel vibrations describe a longitudinal wave, whereas a transverse wave has vibrations perpendicular to energy propagation.
options.C: Any progressive transverse wave reflected back on itself can superpose to form a stationary wave with nodes and antinodes.
options.D: Only electromagnetic transverse waves travel through a vacuum, while mechanical transverse waves such as water or string waves need a medium.
